title: Best Low-Cost Index Funds for Long-Term U.S. Investors
description: A comparison of the titans: Vanguard vs. Fidelity vs. Schwab vs. ETFs.
content:
When Jack Bogle launched the first index fund in 1976, Wall Street laughed. They called it 'Bogle's Folly' and said trying to match the market average was un-American. Today, Index Funds have eaten Wall Street. Trillions of dollars have flowed into these boring, low-cost funds because the math is undeniable: 90% of active managers fail to beat the index over 15 years. But with thousands of 'Index Funds' now available, which ones should you buy? This guide compares the specific tickers (VTI, VOO, FZROX, SWTSX) that form the bedrock of a US millionaire's portfolio.

Key Takeaways

  • Total Market vs S&P 500: Total Market funds (VTI) hold ~3,700 stocks (including Small Cap). S&P 500 (VOO) holds ~500. They perform similarly (99% correlation), but Total Market is theoretically safer.
  • Mutual Fund vs ETF: In a Taxable account, ETFs are slightly better. In an IRA/401k, Mutual Funds allow for auto-investing every dollar.
  • The Zero Cost War: Fidelity now offers funds with literally 0.00% fees. This is a loss leader to get your business.
  • Brand Agnostic: A Vanguard S&P 500 fund and a Schwab S&P 500 fund are identical products. Buy the one your broker offers free of transaction fees.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US market is unique in having 'Zero Expense Ratio' funds. Fidelity's FZROX charges $0 on $10,000 invested. Vanguard's VTSAX charges $4. The difference is negligible, but the psychological shift to 'free investing' is powerful.

The Ticker Showdown

Here are the best-in-class funds for each major brokerage. Stick to the 'Home Team' to avoid transaction fees (e.g., buying a Vanguard fund at Fidelity might cost $75).

1. The Vanguard Ecosystem

  • ETF: VTI (Total Stock Market) - 0.03% ER.
  • Mutual Fund: VTSAX (Total Stock Market) - 0.04% ER, $3k min.
  • Verdict: The Gold Standard. VTI is the most popular ETF in the world for a reason.

2. The Fidelity Ecosystem

  • Zero Fund: FZROX (Total Market) - 0.00% ER. (Proprietary index).
  • Traditional Fund: FSKAX (Total Market) - 0.015% ER.
  • Verdict: Use FZROX in an IRA. Use FSKAX in a taxable account (because Zero funds can't be transferred to other brokers).

3. The Schwab Ecosystem

  • Fund: SWTSX (Total Market) - 0.03% ER.
  • ETF: SCHB (Broad Market) - 0.03% ER.
  • Verdict: Excellent. SWTSX has no minimum, unlike VTSAX.

How to Choose Based on Account Type

  1. Roth IRA: Use the Mutual Fund version (VTSAX/FZROX/SWTSX). Why? You can set up 'Automatic Investing' to pull $500 from your bank and buy exactly $500 of the fund automatically. Automation wins.
  2. Taxable Brokerage: Use the ETF version (VTI/SCHB). Why? ETFs are more tax-efficient (no capital gains distributions) and portable (can transfer to any broker).
  3. 401(k): You usually can't pick. Look for 'Institutional Index' or '500 Index'. Check the Expense Ratio. If it's under 0.10%, it's good. If only high-fee active funds are available, lobby your HR department.

Frequently Asked Questions

What about the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ)?

QQQ tracks the top 100 non-financial companies (mostly Tech). It has higher growth but higher volatility. It is not a 'Core' holding like VTI. Treat it as a 'tilt' (maybe 10-20% of portfolio).

Is there a risk to Fidelity Zero funds?

The main risk is 'Lock-In.' You cannot transfer FZROX to Vanguard. You must sell it (triggering taxes) to move. That's why we recommend them only for tax-sheltered accounts (IRAs) where selling is tax-free.

Why do some funds have $3,000 minimums?

Mutual funds have administrative costs. Vanguard wants serious investors. If you don't have $3,000 yet, buy the ETF version (VTI) for the price of 1 share (~$250) or use Fidelity.
